extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature/classical studies; poets and writers interested in poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Aristotle's principles for composing and evaluating poetry and the fine arts (esp. tragedy), as presented and discussed in S. H. Butcher's edition and commentary of the Poetics. Focuses on formal, stylistic, and evaluative criteria (imitation, unity, katharsis, plot, character, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the defining principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ as the common characteristic of the Fine Arts: a current phrase interpreted anew by Aristotle: Poetry is an expression of the ‘universal’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation is not literal copying but a representation of the universal element in human life; art reproduces its original not 'as it is in itself' but as presented to the phantasy. Avoid reading 'imitation' as mere facsimile; treat poetry as idealised representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of aesthetic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of aesthetic imitation are human Character (ethos), Emotion (pathos), and Action (praxis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating, check which of these objects the work targets and how accurately and philosophically the work presents the universal aspects of them (e.g., believable emotions, coherent actions, consistent character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium of imitation in poetry and the arts is Rhythm, Language, and ‘Harmony’ (melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the choice and control of medium (meter, diction, music) and how they serve the representation of the universal; verse and musical elements should support, not obscure, the action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner (mode) of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic, narrative (including lyric), or mixed (drama with song and dancing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the chosen mode (dramatic representation, pure narrative, lyric, or combination) and evaluate consistency and appropriateness of that mode to the material and effect sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic universality vs. historical particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an expression of the 'universal' and therefore different from History; Poetry treats the probable and possible, not merely empirical fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work rises from particulars to reveal universal truths (character types, motives, conditions) rather than merely recounting events; prefer idealised patterning that illuminates the universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth: probability and possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry depends on 'probabilities' and 'possibilities' rather than on literal empirical accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check internal plausibility and how incidents cohere with human nature and the poem's own laws; improbable chance events are to be avoided unless made credible within the work's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of chance/accident in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry excludes the rule of Chance; the plot must have necessity or probability rather than relying on random accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot developments should arise logically from preceding causes, character, or circumstance; avoid deus ex machina or accidental contrivances that undermine organic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of Fine Art: pleasure (two kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Fine Art is pleasure: lower forms give pastime (w aid id), higher forms yield noble enjoyment akin to supreme happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging, distinguish mere entertainment from the higher aesthetic pleasure that refines understanding or emotion; consider whether the work affords noble enjoyment (intellectual/emotional enrichment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of Tragedy: katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy's function is to produce a katharsis of pity and fear — a clarifying or refining of emotion — effected by dramatic means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the play arouses and then purges or purifies pity and fear by means of its plotted events and emotional economy; examine whether the emotional arc leads to insight or emotional clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy consists of six elements: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Thought (dianoia) — the internal elements; and Diction (lexis), Melody (melos), Spectacle (opsis) — the external elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each element but prioritize plotting and the intellectual content; identify strengths and weaknesses in diction, musical elements, and scenic presentation as they relate to the core action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (plot as 'soul' of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the representation of action) is the primary element in tragedy; character and thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plot coherence, causal linkage, and how action shapes meaning; character assessment should be subordinate to how character serves plot and provokes necessary reversals/recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole and of proper magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude — having a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check completeness (no loose threads), sufficient scale to enact the theme, and that the structure supports an organic progression from inciting action to resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action as primary unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the primary unity: tragedy should exhibit one complete action with causally related parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge unity by whether incidents contribute to a single main action; subsidiary episodes must serve the central plot, not distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unities of Time and Place (minor unities)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Unity of Time’ is discussed as an incidental practice of the Greek stage and later became a formal rule; 'Unity of Place' is not mentioned by Aristotle but later deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider time/place compression for idealisation and plausibility, but do not treat strict temporal or spatial coincidence as essential unless it serves unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero (protagonist type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's ideal protagonist is deduced from the function of tragedy to produce pity and fear; tragic protagonists should provoke pity/fear, and certain character-types are excluded (e.g., wholly virtuous or wholly villainous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating a tragic protagonist, ensure they have a moral stature that invites pity when they fall (often through error or frailty) rather than being merely depraved or flawless; allow room for tragic collision and ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (error/fault) and reversal/recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial mechanism is hamartia (error/fault) producing peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition), which together move the plot to its cathartic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess causes of reversal: should be rooted in character or plausible circumstance; recognition should be intelligible and arise naturally from action, enhancing the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) subordinate but essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is secondary to action but intimately related; character (in large sense including ethos and dianoia) must be coherent and fit the actions required by the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters for consistency, suitability to their roles, and ability to illuminate universal human types; character changes should follow from action rather than arbitrary authorial imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (choice of words, expression, names) is one of the external elements and must suit the genre and convey the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge language for appropriateness, clarity, and poetic force (e.g., effective metaphor); in comedy, expressive names may aid generalisation; in tragedy, diction should serve elevated representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (melos) and the role of music/chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (song) and musical elements form a constituent of tragedy and can effect katharsis (including a 'musical katharsis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the contribution of musical elements and chorus to emotional arc and unity: they should integrate with plot and enhance the emotional and universal effects rather than merely ornament the spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (scenic presentment) as external but subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (scenic presentation) is an external element and less artistic in the poet's control; Aristotle treats it as of least importance compared to plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scenic display for appropriateness and effect, but remember that greatness of drama comes from plot and character; spectacle should not compensate for weak plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation and generalisation (comic and tragic modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art idealises: Tragedy idealises persons; Comedy generalises (creates personified ideals); both move from the individual to the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing, see how the work abstracts and idealises particulars into representative types and whether that idealisation is coherent and illuminating rather than caricatured or merely archetypal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral versus aesthetic function
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational (moral) from the aesthetic function of poetry: his critical estimates rest on aesthetic grounds though some rules have moral implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate principally on aesthetic criteria (unity, universality, catharsis), while noting moral effects where Aristotle's rules imply ethical considerations (e.g., propriety of character), but avoid conflating didacticism with artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of taste (xaprels) as standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste (xaprels) is indicated in the work as a controlling standard of aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider prevailing standards of taste and the audience's capacities; judgments of quality should reflect sensitivity to form, proportion, and the noble pleasure Aristotle describes, not merely novelty or shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and verse as components of poetic art
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse (metre) is an element of poetry and contributes to the medium of imitation; rhythm and metre affect the imitative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metrical choices for their aptness to mood, mode, and the universal qualities being represented; rhythm should enhance the phantasy and the emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism: rules as tentative
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's rules are often tentative rather than dogmatic; some rules need revision or qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Aristotle's prescriptions as critically informed guidelines rather than immutable laws; adapt principles to differing materials, historical contexts, and artistic aims while preserving the core concerns (unity, universality, plot integrity).
